title: Policing cross-border fraud ‘Above and below the surface’: mapping actions and developing a more effective global response

sections.name: Início (1/5)
sections.text:
Crime, Law and Social Change (2025) 83:5 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10611-024-10186-2 Abstract Cross-border fraud, including its various forms such as online retail fraud, pyramid schemes, romance fraud and pig butchering, is a major problem around the world. Despite clear evidence that cross-border fraud is growing, there is little research charting the scale of cross-border fraud and the optimal policing responses to deal with it. This paper aims to fill this research gap by exploring what we know about the nature of cross-border fraud and current policing response. Unlike in other crime areas with a cross-border element, international bodies and nation states have shown very little interest in addressing cross-border frauds through what we term the higher profile ‘above the surface’ activities. Instead, policing responses have been present on a much larger scale in the private sector ‘below the surface’, with much less profile. Moreover, the paper argues that while cooperation and coordina - tion between the public and private sector actors is crucial, there are very few po - licing structures bringing these diverse actors together to tackle cross-border fraud, among other gaps. By drawing on examples of alternative structures dealing with cross-border economic crime, the paper informs policy-makers by mapping out key actions and structures which should be considered to better tackle the global problem of cross-border fraud. Keywords Cross-border fraud · Policing · Enforcement · Sanctions · Reform Introduction Fraud is a global problem with significant cross-border activity (Kemp et al., 2020 ; Levi, 2017 ; United Nations, 2023 ). Facilitated by advances in communication technology and globalisation of business, it has become incredibly easy and cheap for fraudsters in one country to target victims in another (Button & Cross, 2017 ; Accepted: 20 December 2024 / Published online: 10 January 2025 © The Author(s) 2024 Policing cross-border fraud ‘Above and below the surface’: mapping actions and developing a more effective global response Mark Button 1  · Branislav Hock 1  · Joon Bae Suh 2  · Chol Soo Koh 3 Extended author information available on the last page of the article 1 3
McGuire, 2017 ). By contrast, cross-border fraud is securing low levels of global reg - ulatory response, compared to international bribery and money laundering (Button et al., 2022 ; Hock, 2020 ). Law enforcement across the world is largely national, limited by jurisdictional, legal, political, and operational barriers (Hock, 2020 ). Besides the European Union’s initiative against certain types of cross-border fraud and a lim - ited activity undertaken by Interpol, other international bodies have shown very little interest in combatting cross-border fraud in comparison to other global crimes (Ligeti et al., 2020 ). There are also some nation states such as the USA and China who have directed more effort at the problem. Together, however, these ‘above the surface’ higher profile state structures dedicated to the problem amount to very little in the face of the size of this problem. There is much more activity confronting this chal - lenge being pursued by private actors ‘beneath the surface’, with much lower profiles among private actors such as companies selling services, global corporations, NGOs and voluntary actors. Furthermore, the lack of policing response goes hand in hand with very little research charting the scale of cross-border fraud and the optimal policing responses to deal with it (Button, 2012 ; Cross, 2020 ; Valentine, 2000 ). This paper aims to fill this research gap by exploring what we know about the nature of cross-border fraud and current policing response. While the paper will not offer the definitive answers, it provides a criminological account based upon the best evidence available. First, the paper will seek to illustrate the depth and ubiquity of cross-border fraud and dem - onstrate who is involved. Second, the paper will juxtapose the ‘friction’ of engag - ing in cross-border fraud, versus that of investigating and prosecuting it. Third, the paper will explore evidence of the extent of investigative activity across borders. Fourth, the paper will examine intergovernmental initiatives addressing the prob - lem, followed by other private and non-governmental responses. Finally, the paper will weave this analysis together to offer some insights on what needs to be done to impact upon cross-border fraud offering a series of activities and roles which need to be undertaken by existing international bodies or potentially new entities. The scale of cross-border fraud Determining how much cross-border fraud can be accounted for is very difficult. It is true that scholars provide strong evidence that fraud is perpetrated on an industrial scale across borders (Carter, 2021 ; Cross, 2020 ; Levi, 2017 ). Yet, efforts to quantify the scale of a problem are hampered by the lack of reliable information from inci - dents of fraud, including the struggle to identify the origin of the fraudulent schemes (as noted by Skidmore et al., 2018 relating organised fraud). This struggle to accu - rately measure the nature of the problem might well explain the relative lack of inter - est of policy-makers to cross-border fraud (Button et al., 2023a , b ). There are, however, some snippets of data from a variety of sources that begin to illustrate the scale of cross-border activity. In the UK, the City of London Police has estimated that 70% of frauds in England and Wales either originate from abroad or have an international element (Home Office, 2023 , p.11). Little detail is offered in this assessment and the ‘international element’ could be the laundering of the funds 5 Page 2 of 27
in another country after the initial domestic fraud. Nevertheless, the statement does show that cross-border fraud accounts for a significant proportion. By contrast the Federal Trade Commission publishes data on cross-border frauds and of the reports it receives in 2022 noted only 11% of fraud reports originating from beyond the USA (albeit based upon where the victim perceived it originated from - which is unlikely to be an accurate measure). These still, nevertheless, amounted to 293,058 frauds, not an insignificant number (Federal Trade Commission, 2023 ). There are other estimates from other countries that illustrate the scale of the prob - lem in particular types of fraud too. In the USA tech support/government imper - sonation phone scams amounted to just over $1 billion of losses to US citizens of which the FBI noted, “The scams primarily emanate from call centers in South Asia, mainly India” (Internet Crime Complaint Center, 2023 , p 16). A report in a newspa - per claimed for six months in 2015 there were 4.7 billion scam calls from Taiwan to China (The Diplomat, 2023 ). A journalist investigating romance scammers in Nigeria estimated there could by hundreds of thousands of them engaged in it and noting a quote from a Yahoo Boy, discovered: “For every successful Yahoo boy that makes $100,000 from a victim and buys a house,” Bukky said, “there are hundreds with a phone in the slums who get no more than a hundred dollars (Barragán, 2023 ). A report on card-not-present fraud in the European Union (EU) estimated the scale of the problem to be €1.28 billion of which 68% of these transactions were cross-border (European Central Bank, n.d. , p. 3). Many cybercrimes overlap with fraud and there is much evidence of the extent of cross-border cybercrime. Industry research has suggested from Russia alone over 8 billion phishing emails are sent out every day (AAG, 2023 ). Analysis of the origin of spam emails by AAG ( 2023 ) also noted: The top 5 countries of origin for spam were Russia (29.82%), Mainland China (14%), the USA (10.71%), Germany (5.19%) and the Netherlands (3.70%). There is substantial evidence of some countries with thousands of dedicated scam - mers and cyber criminals targeting other countries with frauds such as romance, investment (including crypto and ‘pig butchering’ which often combine both), pyra - mid, shopping to identity frauds to name some of the most common (Carter, 2024 ; Whittaker et al., 2023 ; Deliema et al., 2020 ; Hock & Button, 2023a ; Lazarus, 2024 ; Lazarus et al., 2023 ; Nagunwa, 2014 ; Whittaker et al., 2024 ). Nigeria has its Yahoo Boys and many writers have illustrated their ubiquity (Lazarus, 2018 , 2024 ; Leuk - feltd & Holt, 2020 ; Lusthaus et al., 2024 ; Smith, 2006 ) and some have illustrated how normalised such activities have become in broader Nigerian culture (Lazarus et al., 2022 ). Romance frauds and crypto-currency frauds have become the staple of these and other West African fraudsters, but there are no clear estimates of their number (Barnor, 2024 ; Drew & Webster, 2024 ; Interpol, 2020 ; Lazarus, 2024 ). And Nigeria is not alone, Cameroon, for example, has pet scammers targeting other countries (Whittaker & Button, 2020 ), Ghana has the ‘Sakawa Boys’ conducting similar frauds Page 3 of 27 5
to Nigerian scammers (Alhassan & Ridwan, 2023 ), Ivory Coast has the ‘brouteurs’ (Cretu-Adatte et al., 2024 ) and India has tech support and government impersonation scammers, to name some (Datta et al., 2020 ; Internet Crime Complaint Center, 2023 ). South East Asia has also developed an even more disturbing problem of industrial scale scam compounds with forced labour conducting the scamming across borders (Franceschini et al., 2023 ; Sarkar and Shukla, 2024 ; United Nations, 2023 ). This overlap between cybercrimes and cross-border fraud exemplifies some of the concep - tual challenges associated with measuring the scale of cross-border fraud. Furthermore, useful findings about the scale of cross-border fraud can be seen through the lenses of organised crime research. Organised crime has been noted to be a key actor in perpetrating frauds and in some countries their activities have gone to a new level (Crocker et al., 2017 ; Lazaraus, 2024 ; Lusthaus et al., 2023 ; May & Bhardwa, 2017 ). Research and journalistic exposes are increasingly illustrating the huge number of people who are trafficked into slave camps where they are forced to conduct scams predominantly at victims in other countries. A recent UN report estimated there could be as many as 120,000 held in Myanmar and a 100,000 in Cambodia forced into scam operations targeting other South East Asian countries (United Nations, 2023 ). The discussion about the scale of cross-border fraud is closely related to the nature of perpetrators. In this section, we briefly introduce the sole traders, small groups, organised crime groups, and corporate fraudsters as key types of perpetrators based upon the authors assessment of the literature and media reports of convicted fraudsters. Sole traders There are lone fraudsters who target nationals in other countries. In one example the US extradited a Nigerian national from Lagos who was alleged to have defrauded a US citizen in Kentucky of $148,000 (Omolaoye, 2022 ). Small groups There are also numerous examples of small groups of fraudsters, which are not sophisticated criminal enterprises, but rather a group of friends or like minded indi - viduals who work together (Cretu-Adatte et al., 2024 ; Lusthaus et al., 2024 ; Lazarus, 2018 ). In one case three Nigerians were implicated with extradition sought by the US authorities where the victims were for an alleged $6 million business email compro - mise scam, which they had been perpetrating from South Africa (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, 2023 ). Organised crime groups There are also examples of sophisticated organised crime groups using dozens of staff to perpetrate frauds against nationals in other countries. In India call centres are commonly established to target other countries with most commonly tech support scams and impersonation scams (Datta et al., 2020 ). These schemes often involve 5 Page 4 of 27
dozens to hundreds of persons. They do vary on the extent to which operatives are aware they are actively engaged in fraud. In one example in Hyderabad, India, a call centre targeting US citizens was raided by the police and 115 were arrested (Times of India, 2023 ). There is also a growing recognition that Nigerian confraternities, such as Black Axe, which often have thousands of members are also involved in pep - etrating cross-border frauds (Interpol, 2020 ; Lazarus, 2024 ). An even more sinister version of organised crime involvement is also emerging in South East Asia where individuals are offered fake jobs which involve them travelling to another country where they are then placed in camps and forced to scam people with hundreds of thousands estimated to be trapped in Myanmar and Cambodia alone (Franceschini et al., 2023 ; Sarkar and Shukla, 2024 ; United Nations, 2023 ). Other typologies It is also important to note many cross-border frauds are perpetrated by, what seem at least from the outside, lawful businesses. There have been some major scandals involving corporations such as Enron, Worldcom and FTX are just a few high-profile examples to illustrate this. These corporate scandals have caused victims in mul - tiple countries losses. This article is primarily directed at the criminal fraudsters who largely target individuals and businesses, and corporate fraudsters is not the main focus. Another important distinction in exploring these cross-border criminals is between: ● Citizens targeting their home country from another country (British citizen goes to Spain to target British Citizens). ● Citizens from one country moving to another country to target a third country (British citizen goes to Nigeria to target Americans). ● Citizens from one country targeting citizens from another (Indian citizens target British Citizens). Now the scale and nature of cross-border fraud have been illustrated it would be use - ful to explore the barriers to perpetrating and countering cross-border fraud. Friction and engaging with cross-border fraud If one was to travel back 30 years conducting cross-border fraud would have involved a great deal of friction. There would have been significant costs to cover postage, telephone calls and labour to conduct such criminal schemes. A West African fraud - ster, for example, wishing to target European citizens would not only have to face challenges finding large lists of potential victims but they would also have to com - municate with them through the telephone or traditional letters (Button et al., 2009 ). Fast forward to the 2020s, the friction for a fraudster targeting another country is minimal. Bulk email addresses can be easily found and large numbers of emails can be sent with one click of a keyboard. Even phoning potential victims is much more cost effective, as the cost of calls has declined (Button & Cross, 2017 ; McGuire, Page 5 of 27 5
2017 ). One can argue that a challenge is not really defrauding people but when the fraudster has secured the loot and wishes to launder it. Juxtapose that with the law enforcement investigator where there are many barriers (ACPO, 2012 ; AllahRakha, 2024 ; Blažič & Klobučar, 2020 ; and Tóth and Gáspár, 2020 ). Consider the following example illustrating typical challenges faced by policing agencies when facing cross-border fraud. A European police force receive a report from a victim and the initial investigation reveals a strong suspect based in Nigeria (in many cases a clear suspect or location will not be possible). The revelation of a foreign suspect may lead to immediate low priority and no further action because of the perceived barriers. If the investigator does pursue the case, they then have to contact the relevant International Liaison Officer who may also be overwhelmed and not prioritise the case. If they do, they will enable contacts, but the Nigerian police may not see it as a priority. Moreover, they may lack resources and there might be language, political, jurisdictional and other barriers that frustrate any effective action. Should the case still go through and the police receive a positive response from their Nigerian counterparts, the officers then might need to travel to Nigeria with resource implications, which might not be supported. Assuming they are and the police seek information, search and interview the suspect they will need to make requests to the Nigerian police and secure their support and resources to facilitate this. The suspect might be difficult to find and even if they are, they might be unco - operative. If extradition is sought there are procedures to pursue and further resource implications. If the suspect has resources they may fight extradition. This process may take time and be refused. Should the legal circumstances allow the home coun - try of the fraudster to pursue a criminal prosecution, many of the same barriers listed above exist. There is friction at every point in the process and Fig. 1 draws out these key friction points. Figure 1 also juxtaposes the barriers to a cross-border investigation compared to a scammer engaging in fraud. The figure illustrates the many barriers law enforce - ment face compared to the bad actor. Compared to the fraudsters, who face virtually frictionless action, cross-border fraud investigations aimed at a criminal prosecution outcome face significant friction at almost every point in the investigation process, which in the absence of effective international cooperation mechanisms takes very determined and well resourced investigators to overcome. The conseqences of this friction are limited investigations and actions against cross-border fraudsters, which will now be illustrated. Evidence of cross-border investigations Evidence of cross-border fraud investigations by law enforcement would be illus - trated by a range of indicators such as extraditions, sanctions and disruption of for - eign fraudsters. 5 Page 6 of 27
Extradition Extradition is at the high end, is resource intensive and indicates significant inves - tigative activity as investigators would have to find enough evidence on a case to pursue extradition of the suspect(s) (Ajayi, 2016 ). It is only a rough indicator of activity, because some cases might be investigated where thresholds for extradition Fig. 1 Juxtaposition of cross-border fraud and investigations (Using UK as example) Page 7 of 27 5
are not met or the country where the fraudster is based does not have an extradition agreement. Nevertheless, extraditions illustrate investigations of fraud occurring at a cross-border level. While the volume of cross-border fraud provides a potential for many cross-border investigations, evidence from one country where statistics were sought, the UK, indicates very little activity in this area. Table 1 below illustrates the tiny number of cases related to fraud that culminate in an extradition request, literally a ‘handful’ each year with only 16 in the last five years. The freedom of informa - tion (FOI) request also sought the names of the countries where these requests had been targeted, and they included: Canada, Dominican Republic, Pakistan, Singapore, South Africa, Switzerland, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, the United States and Zambia. Some of the countries where there are high volumes of frauds originating against the UK are missing such as Nigeria and India. It is difficult to determine the extent of extradition activity in other countries directed at cross-border frauds, but there have been some media reports of cases in some nations which illustrate significantly more activity. China has been very effective at securing mass deportations of fraudsters (largely Chinese and Taiwanese nationals) targeting China. The following are an illustration of some news articles illustrating such cases and illustrate Europe, Africa, Oceania and South East Asia as areas where China has been successful. ● 109 fraud suspects deported from Myanmar to Chi

The USA, although not to the same level as China, has also been more active in securing the extradition of suspected fraudsters targeting them from abroad. Many cases can be found, but they tend to be smaller. ● 4 Nigerian nationals based in the UK and Sweden targeting the USA with fraud extradited (United States Attorney’s Office, 2023 ). ● 61 indicted by US authorities for Indian call centre scams targeting the USA with extradition sought for non-US based (Reuters, 2016 ). ● Ghanian social media influencer extradited to the USA in connection with $2 mil - lion romance fraud targeting Americans (NBC News, 2023 ). Some law enforcement bodies might regard extradition as too expensive and time consuming and prefer for local law enforcement to pursue investigations and pros - ecutions. Gathering this data is very difficult as finding information on the involve - ment of foreign law enforcement in countries like Nigeria and Ghana is very difficult. However, it would be likely that UK enforcement (and other countries) would pro - mote any successful co-operation as the local enforcement would. Again there is not much evidence of this either. For example, a search of the UK’s National Crime Agency News section for ‘fraud convictions’ found no relevant local convictions. This could of course be because they are not publicised, but given prior discussion its likely there is also limited activity in this area too. Another indicator of cross-border activity is Interpol Red Notices, which are a request to arrest a person pending an extradition request. These are not perfect as they would also include criminals who have committed a crime in a country and then absconded to another, but they do at least illustrate some cross-border fraud inves - tigative activity. Red Notices can be viewed on the Interpol website and at the time of writing (September 25, 2023) there were 6918 live Red Notices. Refining them by adding ‘fraud’ to the search of them narrowed this down to 164 (Interpol, 2023a ). These can be refined further by searching for the country seeking the person: China was seeking 1, the USA 3, UK and South Korea both 0. An example of a past case illustrating their use is shown in the Interpol annual report: Two suspects wanted in connection with an international Ponzi scheme which defrauded thousands of victims in the Republic of Korea were arrested in Greece and Italy with INTERPOL support. The Polish and German suspects were wanted internationally under INTERPOL Red Notices issued by Korean authorities for their alleged role in the scheme, which embezzled approximately EUR 28 million from around 2,000 Korean victims (Interpol, 2023b , p8). Alternatives to criminal prosecution: sanction regimes, regulatory fines, and civil justice An alternative to seeking criminal prosecution which has been used for some eco - nomic crimes in an international context are sanctions (restrictive measures), regu - latory fines, and civil proceedings (Hock, 2020 ; Rose, 2015 ; Teichmann & Sergi, 2018 ). For both individuals and organisations, these involve, for example, bans on Page 9 of 27 5
financial institutions to process any fraudsters’ transactions, civil recovery orders on suspected fraudster’s assets, out-of-court settlements, and financial penalties. They are also usually associated with a lower burden of proof at the civil and regulatory levels, rather than criminal law level. There are a variety of these alternatives to criminal prosecutions that cut across economic crimes which could be applied to cross-border fraudsters: ● Anti-money laundering (AML) regime (laws allowing the recovery of proceeds of most frauds); ● Cyber-sanctions regime (penalising hacking-related frauds); ● International bribery laws (penalising procurement fraudsters who bribe foreign public officials not intervene; settling out-of court with corporate offenders); ● Global human rights sanctions (trafficking of people to be forced to scam) (House of Commons Library, 2022 ). There are no specific global sanctions and fine regimes for cross-border frauds. The above would cover many aspects, but the lack of a specific regime is a gap. Large num - bers of individuals and corporations have been sanctioned under the above regimes (as well as others), but there is little evidence of their use against cross-border fraud - sters. For example, a map of the world produced by the UK Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office ( 2022 ) shows no restrictions on financial transactions and similar restrictive measures against individuals or organisations from Ghana, Nigeria or India, countries where there are large numbers of active cross-border fraudsters. The National Crime Agency in the UK, which leads in this area in the UK, has sanc - tioned economic criminals. For example, in 2023 a joint effort between the UK/USA sanctioned 7 Russians involved in ransomware attacks (National Crime Agency, 2023 ), but no fraudsters based in the high volume fraud countries. Sanctions and fines for dealing with cross-border fraud are a significantly under-developed area. This is something this paper will further discuss later. Disruption Another aspect of alternatives to criminal prosecution are disruption activities such as closing down telephone lines, websites, email addresses, social media profiles and bank accounts to name some of the most common related to this area (Clough, 2020 ; Himma, 2008 ; Skidmore, 2023 ). Law enforcement agencies across the globe clearly engage in these types of activities, but it is very difficult to determine the extent of them. The data which is available makes it difficult to provide an accurate estimate of cross-border fraud investigations by law enforcement. However, the brief illustration of evidence above shows that set against the scale of the size of cross-border fraud only a tiny number of cases are investigated. Like so many issues in cross-border fraud, more research is required to explore this. This paper will now move on to explore the different entities engaged in policing cross-border fraud. 5 Page 10 of 27
International and national policing responses The response to cross-border can be visualised by those activities ‘above the surface’ which can be easily viewed and those ‘beneath the surface’ which remain largely hidden. The work of international organisations and certain key national state agen - cies active in this area can be viewed as the ‘above the surface’ element. It is largely observable with key publicly available evidence of what they are doing, but in terms of the scale of the problem doesn’t amount to much. By contrast, as will be seen in the ‘beneath the surface’ section, there is a huge amount of activity largely undertaken by non-state actors. This activity is largely hidden, either because such bodies don’t publicise what they do or they do so in a way which makes it hard to see their work. This area of private policing has been rarely researched, with most studies focused upon transnational security companies (Johnston, 2002 ; Van Steden & De Waard, 2013 ) or broad overviews of involvement (Button, 2019 ). The ‘above the surface’ state initiatives will now be considered. ‘Above the surface’ There are many crimes that involve cross-border activity that have secured signifi - cant intergovernmental responses such as illicit drugs and terrorism (Andreas & Nadelmann, 2008 ; Deflem, 2006 ). Some economic crimes have also secured global responses (Rose, 2015 ). Corruption has secured two international conventions on corruption: the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention and Working Group on Bribery and the United Nations Convention Against Corruption. Money laundering has secured international attention through Conventions such as the United Nations Convention against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances and United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime and the Protocols Thereto related to the proceeds of crime. The global response to money launder - ing has also been galvanised by the Financial Action Task Force setting standards on money laundering prevention and promoting the prevention of the crime (Rose, 2015 ). One important element international conventions bring is common offences and terminology. There is no specific Convention related to fraud, but there is the Buda - pest Convention on Cybercrime 2001 and a Draft United Nations Convention on Countering the Use of Information and Communications Technologies for Criminal Purposes. Some of the provisions in these touch on fraud, but what would be consid - ered cyber-dependent frauds (via hacking, malware etc.), rather than the more ubiq - uitous cyber-enabled frauds (emails, bogus websites, social media etc.). The draft UN Convention also has a focus on cyber-dependent fraud. Despite some of the above harmonisation efforts, the nature of fraud means there are many definitions and types; there is the criminal, civil regulatory blur and some offences are not clearly illegal in all countries. For example, regarding the pyramid scheme fraud, some countries, like Australia, consider the vast majority of pyramid scheme participants to be offenders. Others, such as the US, treat those same people as victims who deserve compensation for the financial harm they have suffered (Hock & Button, 2023b ). Hence, the simple question of whether the act of a fraudster in country A targeting country B is an Page 11 of 27 5
offence in country A/B is not always clear. Furthermore, there are also complex juris - dictional questions. For example, the US Department of Justice is well known for using extraterritorial jurisdiction against non-US based fraudsters and bribers, while the majority of other countries would not have jurisdiction in equivalent cases (Hock & Barrett, 2023b ). Another example includes the questions of victims, when victims in one jurisdiction are often sent to other jurisdictions to seek protection, based on a variety of factors such as where the money went; where the offender was believed to have resided; or where a business or organisation was registered (Cross, 2020 ). There is no specific global anti-fraud body, but there is capacity of varying depth in international organisations. The most important intergovernmental organisation in relation to fraud is Interpol, which has established the Interpol Financial Crime and Anti-Corruption Centre (IFCACC) as part of its structure. This centre has three broad areas of action: fraud and payment crime, anti-money laundering and asset recovery and anti-corruption. Figure 2 below notes the following key areas of activity for IFACC. Interpol and its role in combatting fraud, like so many other bodies, has been the subject of very little scholarship (Agung, 2022 ). Interpol, in addition to facilitating the capture of criminals that have either engaged in cross-border crime or escaped across borders, also operates a number of important databases related to fraud. These include: Fig. 2 Interpol Financial Crime and Anti-Corruption Centre activities. Interpol ( 2022 ) 5 Page 12 of 27
 ● SLTD database (travel and identity documents): records of stolen, lost or invalid travel and identity documents. ● Stolen Administrative Documents (SAD): records of stolen official documents such import/export documents and vehicle registrations. ● Frontex INTERPOL Electronic Library Document System (FIELDS): key mark - ers that indicate counterfeit documents. ● Edison (Electronic Documentation and Information System on Investigation Net - works) examples of genuine documents that enable comparison (INTERPOL, n.d. ). The activities of Interpol illustrate some important work in facilitating cross-border fraud investigations and some of the operations above illustrate the good work which can be done. However, the total staff of Interpol is only 1081 and many of these work on administration roles and some of the many other crimes Interpol deals with, such as: drug trafficking, terrorism, human trafficking, firearms trafficking, war crimes to name some (INTERPOL, 2023b , p30). Even if all of the INTERPOL staff were dedi - cated to fraud it would not be enough given globally there are millions of cross-bor - der frauds occurring yearly from probably hundreds of thousands of criminal actors. There are also clearly some major gaps: ● A global forum that brings main global actors together to counter fraud from law enforcement, private sector and NGOs to share information and develop strate - gies to combat cross-border fraud. ● Database of fraud intelligence fed from all members and key private and NGO actors. ● Significant disruptive activity against fraudsters: closure of bank accounts, tel - ephone lines, websites, social media accounts etc. ● Significant volume of cross-border investigations co-ordinated. ● Pursuit of alternative sanctions and disruption. ● Significant numbers of forums, events and training provision related to counter - ing cross-border fraud. Interpol also illustrates some other significant global joint initiatives to tackle fraud in its annual report (2023, p7): OPERATION FIRST LIGHT 2022: 76 countries took part in an international clampdown on the organized crime groups behind telecommunications and scamming fraud, particularly telephone deception, romance scams and e-mail deception. 1,770 locations raided worldwide, USD 50 million worth of illicit funds intercepted, 4,000 bank accounts frozen, 2,000 operators, fraudsters and money launderers arrested. OPERATION HAECHI: III Fraud investigators in 31 countries worked together to intercept money and virtual assets linked to a wide range of cyber- enabled financial crimes and money laundering, assisting countries to recover Page 13 of 27 5
and return illicitly obtained funds to victims. USD 130 million worth of assets seized, 975 individuals arrested, 2,800 bank and virtual-asset accounts blocked. OPERATION JACKAL: This joint law enforcement effort mobilised 14 coun - tries across four continents in a targeted strike against Black Axe and related West-African organised crime groups. These groups are responsible for the majority of the world’s cyberenabled financial fraud as well as many other seri - ous crimes. EUR 1.2 million intercepted in bank accounts, 75 arrests, 7 INTER - POL Purple Notices detailing modus operandi, 6 INTERPOL Red Notices for wanted persons. We also see several regional counter-fraud state initiatives. Perhaps, the most effec - tive international legal regime against cross-border fraud represents the EU. While the competence of the EU Institutions has been historically limited in the area of criminal law, the Member States have been gradually transferring to the EU some major competences in the counter-fraud area. This includes: ● The so-called Euro-Crimes, including fraud and money laundering. Directive 2017/1371 (2017) on the fight against fraud to the Union’s financial interests provides a definition of fraud. ● The protection of the EU’s financial interests from fraud. The EU has a vital inter - est to protect its financial interests and its budget, including both the revenue and expenditure sides. ● Elimination of cross-border fraud undermining the EU’s internal market, includ - ing market competition and free movements. Economic crimes such as cartels and fraud in large public procurement projects are sources of unacceptable mar - ket distortions. Unlike in the protection of the EU financial interests, some forms of cross-border fraud threatening the internal market can be directly sanctioned by EU institutions. At the EU level, cross-border fraud is the competence of several EU institutions and bodies. Perhaps the most significant has become the European Public Prosecutor’s Office that focuses on large-scale cross-border fraud and other transnational crimes against the EU budget, as well as (in certain circumstances) other serious cross-bor - der frauds and crimes having cross-border dimension. The EPPO has direct powers to investigate, prosecute and bring to judgement the perpetrators of such offences (Ligeti et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, other EU institutions and bodies include the OLAF, which investigates fraud against the EU budget, the European Court of Auditors, which audits the EU budget in terms of revenue and spending. The EU also has Europol, a supra-national body which encompasses the European Financial and Eco - nomic Crime Center; and Cybercrime Center (Europol, n.d. ). Europol has supported a number of investigations and pursued preventative and disruptive activity related to cross-border frauds such as VAT frauds, airline ticket fraud and consumer frauds. The UNODC is another important international body combating crime, particu - larly cross-border. On its website notes its role has been to, “make the world safer from drugs, organised crime, corruption and terrorism” (UNODC, n.d. ). Fraud is 5 Page 14 of 27
clearly a significant cross-border crime, but the UNODC has shown very little inter - est in it to date and cybercrime - where there are signs of growing attention, has largely focused upon the cyber-dependent and what Ibrahim ( 2016 ) would describe as the psychosocial and geopolitical, rather than socioeconomic types of this crime. The five normative areas of activity of the UNODC has no mention of fraud or even cybercrime (see UNODC, n.d. ). If we consider their list of publications produced since 2000 (at the time of writing in January 2024), not a single publication has fraud in the title or indeed cyber. 1 Further a perusal through the activities of the Open-ended intergovernmental expert group which conducted a comprehensive study of the prob - lem of cybercrime secures barely a mention of cyber-enabled cross-border fraud (see UNODC, 2021 ). One could argue that organised crime, money laundering and cor - ruption which are prominent on the UNODC agenda overlap. But, even if this is the case there is no evidence of significant interest in cross-border cyber-enabled fraud. However, after initial submission of this article in early 2024 the UK Government funded a UNODC initiative to combat organised fraud, which is marking a change in direction and more activity dedicated to this crime problem within the UNODC, including a an amendment to Resolution 78/229 recognising the importance of tack - ling fraud committed by organised crime, among other projects on organised fraud and the legal responses to fraud in different jurisdictions (UNODC, 2024 ). Earlier some of the significant actions of the Chinese and US authorities were also noted, which because of the size, power and reach of these superpowers also look impressive. But the reality is that these efforts amount to the punishment and disruption of a few hundred fraudsters, when there are clearly many thousands (if not more) active globally. These high profile efforts by these key states and international bodies acting in clear view ‘above the surface’ do not amount to much. By contrast, when we consider activities ‘beneath the surface’ conducted by private actors these are much more significant. ‘Beneath the surface’: private actions Beneath the surface there is a huge amount of activity targeting cross

-border frauds being undertaken by private actors (Button, 2020 ). These include: ● Entities offering services to clients to investigate, disrupt and prevent cross-bor - der frauds; ● Large global companies who experience significant levels of cross-border fraud against them. These companies have developed significant capacity to protect themselves, and. ● Non-Governmental Organisations and voluntary actors who fill the policing space left, both intentionally and unintentionally, by public policing, to tackle the problem themselves. 1 See UNODC ( n.d. ). Commercial providers of services There are a wide range of commercial actors who charge fees for services to com - bat cross-border fraud and related activities (Hock & Dávid-Barrett, 2022 ). The key providers include: private investigators, accountants and lawyers who charge fees to victims of cross-border fraud to deal with their case or prevent victimisation (Button et al., 2023a , b ). These include firms specialising in investigating cases, who then depending upon the client’s needs might then pursue civil litigation or hand the case over to law enforcement or regulators. Some of these actors have global capacity that exceeds that of some of the international bodies discussed above. For example the big accountancy firm Deloitte boasts a global forensic team of 1400 in 30 countries (Deloitte, n.d. ) and the investigative firm, Kroll has 6500 staff in 32 countries (Kroll, n.d. ). Much of their work will be based solely in one country but a good proportion of corruption, money laundering and corporate frauds will have a cross-border ele - ment, particularly tracing funds. These two companies are just two examples of many more operating. Many firms experience bad actors creating fake websites to defraud their cus - tomers, sell counterfeit goods or damage their reputation. Consequently, there are firms that specialise in taking down such websites. One company operating in this area – of which there are others – Netcraft, claims to have taken down over 190 mil - lion websites for clients (Netcraft, n.d. ). The cross-over with cyber also brings many cyber security firms who also offer paid services. Online retailers, for example, turn to a wide range of commercial providers to verify how likely the new customer – who might be anywhere in the world – is who they say they are, using a variety of data analytical tools. One of many examples is LexisNexis who in the UK alone in 2022 assessed 15.8 billion transactions identifying 36 million human-initiated fraud attacks and 352 million automated bot attacks of which a significant number of these would have involved a global element (LexusNexus, 2023 ). This sector, however, tends to serve organisations with the resources to pay for their services, rather than individual victims. Transnational corporations There are some transnational corporations operating in multiple countries who because of the nature of their business have developed significant cross-border fraud capacity. The big tech companies like Amazon, Microsoft and Google to name some often have bad actors abusing their services, therefore affecting their reputation or simply have fraudsters impersonating them. The nature of some of their services as platforms for potential fraudsters have also led to governments and regulators pressuring them to do more by adopting new laws and regulations in this area. Such corporations have responded with a wide range of initiatives from high tech solutions that spot potential fraudsters, through to campaigns, litigation, and referrals to law enforcement (Button, 2020 ). For example, Amazon globally has 15,000 working in anti-fraud roles, and in 2022 alone took down over 20,000 phishing websites and 10,000 phone numbers linked to impersonation scams. Amazon has also referred hundreds of bad actors to law enforcement globally (Amazon, 2023 ). In October 5 Page 16 of 27
2023, the Indian Central Investigation Bureau, as a result of work with Amazon and Microsoft, raided 76 suspected illegal call centre locations across India seizing com - puters, phones and detaining suspects (Business Insider, 2023 ). Google also has a large number of staff dedicated to stopping frauds and has taken action in a variety of areas using both tech based solutions as well as pursuing private litigation against bad actors. In one case, a bad actor was sued for creating 350 fake business profiles and over 14,000 fake reviews (Google, 2023 ). There is clearly debate over whether such tech companies are doing enough, but they are clearly very much engaged in both prevention and enforcement against cross-border fraudsters. Voluntary and commercial action It is well documented that private orders step in and offer institutional support in areas beyond the reach of the state (Bernstein, 1992 ; Gomtsian et al., 2018 ). This has also been evidenced in counter-fraud studies, illustrating how private initiatives will fill the gap in addressing a crime problem through: commercial, non-governmental, voluntary and vigilante means (Button, 2019 ; Johnston, 1996 ). Cross-border fraud is no different. The inadequacy of state responses has spawned many initiatives: com - mercial initiatives, global non-governmental initiatives, voluntary action and finally vigilante action. There is not the space to map them all, so this section will just illus - trate significant examples. The resources and activities of some of these bodies far exceed some state organisation’s capacity. There are a variety of global non-governmental organisations who combat fraud. The Global Anti-Scam Alliance is a member based organisation with over 100 mem - ber organisations covering companies like Amazon and NGOs like Cifas. It describes its core mission as: bringing together governments, law enforcement, consumer protection organi - zations, financial authorities and providers, brand protection agencies, social media, Internet service providers and cybersecurity companies to share knowl - edge and define joint actions to protect consumers from getting scammed. It hosts an annual summit, lobbies governments among many other activities (Global Anti-Scam Alliance, n.d. ). The International Consumer Protection and Enforcement Network (ICPEN) is an association of law enforcement and consumer protection organisations from 70 countries representing 5 billion consumers (ICPEN, n.d. ). The key functions ICPEN undertakes includes: ● To co-ordinate and co-operate on consumer protection enforcement matters. ● To share information and intelligence on consumer protection trends and risks. ● To share best practice information about key consumer protection laws, enforce - ment powers and regulatory approaches to consumer protection. ● ICPEN does not deal with the regulation of financial services or product safety (ICPEN, n.d. ). Page 17 of 27 5
The European Association for Secure Transactions (EAST) is a European association of industry and law enforcement members aimed at improving the public/private partnerships in fighting cross-border financial crime related to payments and ATMs (EAST, n.d. ). EAST produces statistical analysis of fraud, issues updates to members and issues alerts among other activities. Telecom networks are commonly used for fraud and the GSMA is a global asso - ciation representing over 1000 mobile phone operators. The organisation provides a fraud intelligence service to its members (GSMA, n.d. ). Another global organisa - tion is ACFE – the Association of Certified Fraud Examiners which has over 90,000 members in 190 chapters worldwide which represents fraud examiners or investiga - tors or those with an interest in fraud (ACFE, n.d. ). Button and Whittaker ( 2021 ) have mapped the wide range of voluntary responses to cyber-fraud and note two major categories of quasi-vigilantism and citizen action. The latter involves groups who bring volunteers together to largely focus on preven - tion oriented activities such as getting fraudulent websites taken down, providing information to citizens and sharing data to name some. One example is Petscams which focuses on these types of consumer scams which occur across the globe. For example, many pet scammers are based in Cameroon and target victims in the USA, Australia and South Africa to name some. Petscams advises potential buyers, gets fraudulent websites taken down and shares its data with key enforcement bod - ies around the world (Whittaker & Button, 2020 ). This illustrates a voluntary body working globally to tackle this type of fraud. By contrast quasi-vigilantism involves the disruption of fraudsters by time-wasting, but also in some cases publicly outing and often humiliating them. The most prominent example of this type of activity is 419Eater.com (Byrne, 2013 ). These scambaiters target fraudsters in other countries. There are a wide range of other lone activities and groups that target these fraudsters, demonstrating cross-border vigilante action. Perhaps the most significant illustration of the work of the scambaiting commu - nity is how feasible and easy cross-border investigations can be. A review of famous scambaiters videos on Youtube, such as Jim Browning and Pierogi (also known as Scammer Paybacks) illustrates not only the time-wasting of scammers but some of the following: ● Hacking of scammers computers (to secure evidence and destroy files to disrupt); ● Hacking of scammers webcams to secure pictures of scammers; ● Hacking of CCTV of scam call centre to observe them; ● Identification of scammers and their leaders; ● Cultivation of insiders as informants; ● Finding locations of scammers workplaces and homes; ● Finding lists of victims and their losses; ● Finding evidence of law enforcement co-operation; ● Forcing scam centres to relocate; ● Co-operation with volunteers and agents cross-borders and agencies; and. ● Securing enough evidence to pass to authorities to secure prosecutions. 5 Page 18 of 27
The success of scambaiters juxtaposed to law enforcement activities illustrates a big gap. The scambaiters are engaging in some activities such as hacking that put them in a difficult legal position, but in reality they are justified when they are targeting clearly active fraudsters. Law enforcement with many advantages of special powers and privileges could clearly learn much from this community in conducting cross- border investigations should their governance structures allow them to ethically pur - sue such activities. There are also some national bodies that take a global approach and don’t just focus upon their own country. A prominent example of this is the US government’s Consumer Sentinel Network. This provides a tool which enables analysis to take place by members of data-reports relating to a wide range of scams and consumer related problems which have been reported to it or its members. The members are largely American law enforcement and consumer agencies, but also some from Aus - tralia and Canada. Some major US and global companies are also linked to the net - work (Federal Trade Commission, n.d. ). Mind the gap: the need for a stronger international response The analysis above naturally leads to this next section which will outline some of the steps that need to be undertaken. This paper has illustrated that there is a significant problem across the globe of cross-border fraud, that it is easy for fraudsters to perpe - trate, and that it is very difficult for national law enforcement bodies to respond. It has also illustrated the ‘above the surface’ activity of the international bodies and some key national bodies ultimately against the scale of the problem is very little. The paper also showed that ‘beneath the surface’ there is a substantial private response to the problem of cross-border global fraud. Assessing this network of actors and assessing the problem there are some clear gaps in the response to global cross-border fraud: ● Gaps in knowledge on the scale and nature of cross-border frauds; ● A lack of networks and forums that bring together actors from above and beneath the surface together to counter cross-border fraud; ● Globally recognised accreditations, training and education that provide a cur - rency of recognition for all actors; ● A lack of global intelligence; ● A sanctions and disruption system targeted at cross-border fraud bad actors; ● Global bodies such as th UNODC having a well resourced programme targeted at cross-border frauds; ● Capacity for cross-border investigations. To address these gaps, there are already a variety of bodies, some already working on fraud, with the potential to do more, and others which should put counter-fraud higher on their agendas. There is also the potential to create a new international organisation (Button, 2012 ), but it is perhaps better to start from the premise of what needs to be done in cross-border fraud, and only then discuss appropriate institutional design. Page 19 of 27 5
Greater global co-ordination and co-operation There are so many actors in international, state and private capacities combating fraud. An important starting point is to create a network and forum that brings the main actors together and quickly enables actors to find others in different countries and organisations. The following is therefore needed: ● A global entity that provides a forum bringing main global actors together coun - tering fraud from law enforcement AND private sector to develop a strategy to combat cross-border fraud. ● A network of accredited individuals globally in the public and private sectors who can easily find one another and work to common standards and terminology making working together easier. ● A programme of training and education for this global community that equips them with the very latest knowledge on the nature of fraud and how to combat it. ● The accreditation of other training providers to upskill and support those involved in combating cross-border fraud. ● A programme of forums, events and conferences provision related to countering cross-border fraud. ● Conduct relevant research that supports the needs of combating cross-border fraud. This could be undertaken by a range of existing organisations together or in combina - tion such as Interpol, UNODC or a new body. The UNODC or the OECD might be well placed to co-ordinate a new convention on cross-border fraud which would also be desirable to galvanise state responses. Greater global enforcement: prosecutions The ultimate sanction for criminal behaviour are criminal sanctions. This paper has illustrated that not enough of this is happening. Interpol is already co-ordinating activities in this area and it would seem they are best placed for this role. However, they need to do more and engage even more with private entities. States also need to provide more adequate funds for them to continue this work and for more cross- border investigations to occur. Perhaps the most powerful in terms of direct powers to investigate, prosecute and bring to judgement the perpetrators of cross-border fraud is the EU’s EPPO, and the application of this model should be explored outside the EU’s remit. Greater global enforcement: sanctions and disruption Securing successful prosecutions for cross-border frauds and the related challenges of extradition are extremely difficult. An alternative to criminal prosecutions are sanction regimes, regulatory fines, and civil justice. As was noted earlier, many of those alternatives have been effectively used in other economic crime regimes, but a specific regime implementing some of those alternatives for cross-border frauds 5 Page 20 of 27
specifically should be created. This includes specific measures related to freezing of fraud-related assets, financial penalties, and fraud specific restrictive measures. The restrictive measures should be applied to the entities that may support criminal net - works perpetrating cross-border frauds, such as: banks, internet providers, telecoms, corrupt officials etc. If it is not possible to prosecute fraudsters, these alternatives could partially fill current policing gaps. For setting standards of such alternatives, which would like to both public and private actors, a new body similar to the Finan - cial Action Task Force or even a sub-division of it should be considered. Furthermore, there is also a place for even more disruption. The small but high profile actions of celebrity scambaiters illustrates the significant actions that can be undertaken to disrupt them. A package of disruptions such as the following could be pursued: ● Closure of websites, social media accounts, email accounts and telephone num - bers. ● Freezing of bank accounts. ● Proactive cyber disruptions (malware on fraudsters computers, doxing fraudsters etc.) ● Organised time wasting. ● Naming and shaming of bad actors. There are probably many more that could be pursued. It is also important that pri - vate actors who do this work do so in an appropriate ethical framework as there has been evidence of some pursuing inappropriate actions. Some form of standards and accreditation in addition to the coordination would also be required. This coordina - tion and accreditation could be undertaken by many organisations but co-ordination and strong networks are important. It is perhaps best placed with the new sanction organisation above. Global intelligence Last is probably the most difficult. Clearly there is a need to collate and share intel - ligence on cross-border fraud at a global level. States are often very reluctant to share intelligence, so this is very likely to be achieved at a global level and at best in smaller trusted groups, such as the five eyes. However, a global entity that collects basic intelligence and information related to emerging scams and shares alerts and data with appropriate networks could perhaps be achieved and built into the work of a body such as Interpol. Conclusion This paper has demonstrated that although there is a lack of high quality data on the nature and extent of cross-border frauds, it is a significant problem worldwide. It illustrated the substantial friction to prosecuting cross-border fraudsters in compari - son to the ease of action for the bad actors. This and other factors has contributed Page 21 of 27 5
to a law enforcement response in most countries which has been slow to offer the necessary resources and actions to tackle the problem. The paper explored the ‘above the surface’ activities of some of the main international organisations, such as Inter - pol and the EU and some key national bodies, such as the FBI. This more ‘visible’ action was illustrated to be very small against the scale of the problem. Juxtaposed to this ‘visible’ activity above the surface, the paper examined the substantial activities of private actors such as commercial firms, global companies, NGOs and voluntary citizens in addressing this problem. These ‘beneath the surface’ actors are more hid - den in what they do to counter cross-border fraud, but what they do adds up to a significant amount of activity. The paper then drew together some of the key gaps in the international response to cross-border fraud and then set out a set of activities/ roles that existing and perhaps new organisations should pursue to better tackle this problem weaving the multiplicity of global, state and private actorsbetter together in a more coordinated and smart response. Writing this paper the authors concluded that presently the skilled bad actors per - petrating cross-border fraud have little concern over apprehension and extradition. Only a tiny number of bad actors are ever apprehended and extradited to the country of their victims. There are other disruptive actions emanating from the ‘beneath the surface’ by

largely private actors which force them to alter their modus operandi, but this is clearly not enough to stem the rise in fraud most countries have been expe - riencing. Those policy-makers considering this problem for the medium and longer term need to grapple with new thoughts, strategies and structures to tackle this prob - lem, that will require radical new ideas and approaches which are currently out of the ‘comfort zone’ of existing thinking and practice. It is hoped this paper offers some of those ideas and forms the basis for the start of a debate on a better international response to the problem.
